review.title: Fix triangular helpers for adjoint Cholesky factors on Julia 1.13
review.head: f4f30f5b0b35ca4069f349804fe7624caa2868f3

body:
On Julia 1.13, `C.U` of a Cholesky factorisation stored as the lower triangle is a non-copying `UpperTriangular(C.factors')` (JuliaLang/LinearAlgebra.jl#1186), so `parent(C.U)` is an `Adjoint`. `upper_triangular` used `convert(typeof(A), UpperTriangular(A))`, which cannot convert to an `Adjoint`, so `cholesky_upper` throws a `MethodError`:

```julia
Bijectors.upper_triangular(parent(cholesky(Hermitian([2.0 1; 1 2], :L)).U))  # MethodError on 1.13
```

Mooncake's forward-mode `cholesky` always stores the lower triangle, so `CorrBijector` and `VecCorrBijector` fail under it; in CI this shows as three `VecCorrBijector` and `cholesky_upper` cases of the Mooncake integration tests on Julia 1.13. `lower_triangular` has the same defect for factors stored as the upper triangle. Both helpers now use `triu` and `tril`. Adds a regression test and a 0.16.4 HISTORY entry.

Stacked on #489, which bumps to 0.16.4 and fixes the ReverseDiff extension and doctests that fail on `main`.

records.body:
(Port of https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/pull/42920)

In master, accessing fields L or U of Cholesky or CholeskyPivoted calls copy() on the transpose. Here I add tests thayt check that the accessors don't allocate more memory than is needed for e.g. the Adjoint() construction, and remove the unnecessary copy(). Generally julia seems to be trying hard to avoid unnecessary allocations, so I would consider this to be a bugfix, not a breaking change.

There is a related discourse thread: https://discourse.julialang.org/t/implementation-for-accessing-cholesky-factors/56219

Side note 1: there is also a copy() in the definition of _chol!(A::AbstractMatrix, ::Type{UpperTriangular}) - it's a bit less clear to me in what cases this will get run and whether it's okay to remove the copy(), so let me know if you think it'd be worth spending the time to go deeper into that also.

Side note 2: some of the code tests uplo using Cuplo === char_uplo(d), some of it using sym_uplo(Cuplo) == d, is there any particular reason for this, or would it be worth unifying it?

records.body:
With ReverseDiff 1.18.8, `BijectorsReverseDiffExt` fails to precompile (`UndefVarError: pd_from_upper not defined`). The extension declared `@grad_from_chainrules` rules for `pd_from_upper`, `_link_chol_lkj_from_upper` and `_link_chol_lkj_from_lower` without importing them; up to 1.18.7 these defined unused local functions, but 1.18.8 (JuliaDiff/ReverseDiff.jl#328) requires the functions to exist. Deleting the rules keeps current behaviour: ReverseDiff gradients match `main` for the affected bijectors on Julia 1.12.

The `find_alpha` rule now computes its partials in the pullback from the current inputs, removing the `tape has finished recording` error on ReverseDiff 1.18.4+ and wrong gradients when a tape is reused at a new input. It also accepts untracked arguments, so reusing a tape with untracked `PlanarLayer` parameters no longer raises a `MethodError`. The `link` and `invlink` doctests no longer print a `LogNormal`, whose display changed in Distributions. Bumps to 0.16.4.

Mooncake CI failed tests are unrelated.

discussion.body: I opened this PR as suggested by @dlfivefifty in the linked discourse thread (which I found following discussion with @KristofferC) and tagging the people who also reviewed #38389: @Keno, @dkarrasch.
I believe this makes the return type a `Union` and that the original motivation for the copy was to have a concrete return type.

> I believe this makes the return type a `Union` and that the original motivation for the copy was to have a concrete return type.

If you think this change should not get merged, because having a concrete return type is the most important consideration, then I can change it to add a comment that explains the reasons for explicit copy, plus making this more explicit in the docstrings (which currently give no indication at all that accessing a field would involve allocations, which I would argue is very counter-intuitive behaviour - property getters shouldn't add any overhead!).

A (higher effort, probably breaking, perhaps cleaner overall) change to get both performance (minimal allocations) and a concrete return type would be to turn `uplo` from a field into a type parametrization.

I think this can mostly be fixed with documentation. You can specify if you want the `L` or the `U` version when you compute the factorization and then you just need to use the same one when extracting the factor.

> You can specify if you want the `L` or the `U` version when you compute the factorization and then you just need to use the same one when extracting the factor.

That's assuming that you're both in control of the code constructing the factorization, and in the code using it. Which is not necessarily the case in practice. E.g. I have code that gets passed an `MvNormal` (from Distributions.jl) whose covariance is a `PDMat` (from PDMats.jl) which contains a Cholesky, and I don't actually get to say whether that Cholesky uses L- or U-representation. 
It's possible of course to write my own function that checks the `uplo` field and returns either `L` or `U'` depending on which is more efficient - as is done in https://github.com/JuliaStats/PDMats.jl/blob/master/src/chol.jl - but I also just identified a bug in that code (https://github.com/JuliaStats/PDMats.jl/issues/143). Would be much nicer if the stdlib made it easy doing the right thing!

We have moved the LinearAlgebra stdlib to an external repo: https://github.com/JuliaLang/LinearAlgebra.jl

@st-- If you think that this PR is still relevant, please open a new PR on the [LinearAlgebra.jl](https://github.com/JuliaLang/LinearAlgebra.jl) repo.

records.body:
For a `Cholesky` factorization, `getproperty` is defined like this:
```julia
function getproperty(C::Cholesky, d::Symbol)
    Cfactors = getfield(C, :factors)
    Cuplo    = getfield(C, :uplo)
    if d === :U
        return UpperTriangular(Cuplo === char_uplo(d) ? Cfactors : copy(Cfactors'))
    elseif d === :L
        return LowerTriangular(Cuplo === char_uplo(d) ? Cfactors : copy(Cfactors'))
    elseif d === :UL
        return (Cuplo === 'U' ? UpperTriangular(Cfactors) : LowerTriangular(Cfactors))
    else
        return getfield(C, d)
    end
end
```
Sometimes this makes a copy, and sometimes it doesn't. As @chriselrod pointed out in [this Zulip discussion](https://julialang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/228422-linear-algebra/topic/.60getproperty.60.20of.20Cholesky.20makes.20a.20copy), this seems to be for type stability, because we don't statically know whether the representation is upper or lower triangular. Without the `copy`, we'd sometimes have an `Adjoint`.

`Cholesky` is defined as
```julia
struct Cholesky{T,S<:AbstractMatrix} <: Factorization{T}
    factors::S
    uplo::Char
    info::BlasInt

    function Cholesky{T,S}(factors, uplo, info) where {T,S<:AbstractMatrix}
        require_one_based_indexing(factors)
        new(factors, uplo, info)
    end
end
```

It would seem we could get type stability without needing to copy if this were changed to
```julia
struct Cholesky{T,S<:AbstractMatrix, UL} <: Factorization{T}
    factors::S
    info::BlasInt

    function Cholesky{T,S}(factors, uplo, info) where {T,S<:AbstractMatrix}
        require_one_based_indexing(factors)
        UL = Symbol(uplo)
        new{T,S,UL}(factors, info)
    end
end
```
Now we know statically how to interpret `factors`, so we know statically whether `C.L` will return a `Matrix` or `Adjoint`.

Alternatively, this information could be stored in the `S` type parameter. Currently this seems to be "forgetful":
```julia
julia> Cholesky(LowerTriangular(randn(3,3))) |> typeof
Cholesky{Float64, Matrix{Float64}}
```

Making `S` be `LowerTriangular{Float64, Matrix{Float64}}` instead of `Matrix{Float64}` would have the same benefits.

The `copy` has been removed in https://github.com/JuliaLang/LinearAlgebra.jl/pull/1186.

As for type stability, Claude recommends to not do anything about it. The reason being that the `uplo` value is a runtime info, that comes from `Hermitian` and isn't a type-parameter there either. So this would become a runtime type parameter, which probably isn't any better than the small (inferred !) union that we currently have. I suggest to close this as not planned.

records.body:
Fixes #314, fixes #315, fixes #319, fixes #320.

`@grad_from_chainrules` reuses the imported signature's argument list in value positions — both in the forwarding call to `ReverseDiff.track` and in the `args = (...)` tuple. A type annotation means something different there, so several signature shapes were broken:

| Shape | Symptom |
|---|---|
| `f(x::TrackedArray, ys::T...)` | `TypeError: expected T, got a value of type Tuple{T, T}` — the collected varargs are asserted against the element type. Also hit with *zero* varargs (`Tuple{}`). |
| `f(x::TrackedArray, ys::T...)` | `T` was never escaped, so it resolved in ReverseDiff's scope: `UndefVarError` for any user-defined type (#319). |
| `f(x::TrackedArray, y::Int = 2)` | The default made it into call position, where `track(f, x, y = 2)` passes `y` as a *keyword* argument. |
| `f(x::TrackedArray; k = 1)` | `_make_fwd_args` rewrote the `:parameters` expression in place, and all three argument lists share it, so the declared defaults were dropped. |

Only untyped `args...` — the one form the tests covered — was unaffected.

## Approach

The macro now builds the generated argument lists directly from `MacroTools.splitdef`/`splitarg`/`combinearg`, and `_make_fwd_args` is removed. The forwarding call and the `args` tuple use argument names only.

Everything user-supplied in the signature is escaped — the function, `where` parameters, argument names, types and defaults — while the macro's own locals rely on standard hygiene. So a user argument named `kwargs`, `args` or `back` cannot clash with them. Because escaped argument names could shadow an escaped reference to the function in a method body, both generated definitions bind the function through its type instead (`(func::_selftype(f))(...)`, `track(func::_selftype(f), ...)`). `_selftype` returns `Type{T}` for a type `T` and `typeof(f)` otherwise, like ChainRulesCore's helper of the same name: `typeof` would give `DataType` for constructors, and `Core.Typeof` is renamed in Julia 1.14.

## Also in here

- **`where` clauses are supported (#320).** The escaped static parameters are attached to the generated definitions. Works whether the parameter appears in the tracked argument (`x::TrackedArray{V}`), only in an untracked one (`y::AbstractVector{V}`), only in an argument with a default (`y::V = 2`), only in a keyword argument (`k::V = 1`), carries a bound (`V <: Real`), or is used only in the bound of another parameter (`where {T, S <: TrackedArray{T}}`). `track` and the `special_*_exec!` methods only see positional types, so they get only the parameters that positional types refer to, directly or through bounds; otherwise Julia warns about unused type variables.
- **A pullback returning the wrong number of tangents now throws (#315).** The old `@assert input_derivs isa Tuple` only checked the type, and tuple broadcasting silently expands a length-1 tuple across every argument — so a pullback returning too few tangents assigned its *first* tangent to *every* argument. The same check now applies to `@grad`. For rrule pullbacks the expected length includes the tangent of the function itself.
- **Zero tangents for tracked arguments no longer error (#314).** `NoTangent()`/`ZeroTangent()` from an rrule and `nothing` from a `@grad` pullback reached `increment_deriv!`, which has no method for them. They are now no-ops.
- **Constructors get their own special instructions (related to #316).** For a type, `SpecialInstruction`'s function parameter was `DataType`, so the `special_*_exec!` methods of two constructors with the same positional signature overwrote each other — an error during package precompilation. `_SpecialInstruction` now uses `_selftype(func)`, and both macros dispatch on `SpecialInstruction{_selftype(f)}`. `@grad` also uses `_selftype` for its `track` method, so it works for constructors too. No built-in instruction records a type, so only user rules are affected.
- **Signatures without positional arguments are rejected.** Keyword arguments do not take part in dispatch, so `@grad_from_chainrules f(; k::TrackedArray)` replaced the original `f(; k)`, and the rrule then recursed into it.
- The docstring documents that overlapping imported signatures need the fully tracked combination imported too, or the generated `special_*_exec!` methods are ambiguous.

## Note for reviewers

The `f_vararg` and `f_kw` rrules in `test/ChainRulesTests.jl` returned two tangents for four arguments and passed only because the varargs were untracked `Int`s that hit the `_add_to_deriv!(d1, d2) = nothing` fallback. They now return the missing `NoTangent()`s. That was a latent wrong-gradient bug, not a regression from this PR.

The stricter length check is a behaviour change for rules that return short tangent tuples: they now error instead of being silently broadcast. `@grad` is not public API, but it is used downstream, so I checked the `@grad` rules in the registered packages GitHub code search finds using it (Tullio, DiffEqBase, NonlinearSolveBase, SimpleNonlinearSolve, Bijectors, SphericalFunctions, ADEV): all of them return one tangent per argument.

`@grad` with qualified names (#318) is out of scope here and left for a follow-up that moves `@grad` to the same approach.

## Tests

New cases in `test/ChainRulesTests.jl`:

- typed varargs with a user type (zero and two varargs)
- pullbacks returning too few tangents or a non-tuple, for both macros
- keyword defaults (the rrule uses a *different* default, so a dropped signature default is visible)
- positional defaults
- zero tangents for tracked arrays and scalars, including `nothing` from `@grad`
- `where` clauses in six shapes, with `@test_nowarn` for the unused type variable warnings
- constructors (`Doubled(x::TrackedArray)`), including a second constructor with the same signature (no method overwrite), a `@grad` constructor, and that constructors of other types are unaffected
- qualified function names
- argument names that coincide with the function or with internal names
- invalid signatures, including keyword-only ones, with their error messages
